passage:
Sick-room note, Tuesday — Deepika Ma'am, school nurse
Trisha (Class 10) came in at lunch saying she felt sick. She had not eaten anything yet. A friend had told her the canteen rajma "makes everyone throw up" and that three children were ill last week. She was pale, breathing fast, one hand on her stomach, and said it started "turning" as soon as she smelled the food. No fever. I checked the canteen log: no illness reported this term. I told her so, sat with her, and we did slow breathing together. After a while she asked for her tiffin. I explained that worry can create real feelings in the stomach, what we call the nocebo effect, and asked her to tell her parents and see their doctor if the sickness keeps coming back.

qa.q: What did the canteen log show?
qa.a: No illness reported this term.

qa.q: Why did Trisha feel her stomach "turning" before eating anything?
qa.a: She expected the rajma to make her sick after what her friend said, and that anxious expectation created real queasy feelings before any food.

qa.q: Which step by Deepika Ma'am helped most, and why?
qa.a: Checking the canteen log and sharing the facts while sitting with Trisha and breathing slowly. It calmed the fear causing the nausea, and she still advised a doctor if it kept happening.

qa.q: What would change if the nurse had just told Trisha it was all in her head?
qa.a: Trisha might feel dismissed and embarrassed, stay scared of the canteen, and be less likely to report real symptoms in future.

grounding: A school nurse notes a teenager who felt nauseous before eating because she had been told the canteen food makes people sick.

passage:
Friday, 9:40 p.m.
Dear diary, today was so weird. At breakfast Darshan said the new mess cook's upma gave half of B-block food poisoning. By lunch I was already queasy. I sat in front of my lemon rice and my stomach literally flipped. I didn't eat a single spoon. Then Warden Ma'am announced that the "food poisoning" was a stomach bug in one room, nothing to do with the mess. And the WEIRDEST part? I stopped feeling sick. Just like that. So was it ever real? It felt real! We learned about the nocebo effect in psych club last month, and I laughed at it then. Not laughing now. Had the rice at dinner. Totally fine.
Urmila

qa.q: What did Warden Ma'am announce?
qa.a: That the "food poisoning" was a stomach bug in one room, nothing to do with the mess.

qa.q: Why was Urmila so confused, asking "So was it ever real?"
qa.a: The sickness felt completely real, yet it vanished once the fear was gone, so Urmila is puzzled that a worry alone could make the stomach flip. 🤔

qa.q: What could Urmila do next time someone warns that the mess food makes people ill?
qa.a: Check with the warden or someone who would actually know before letting the story sink in, and notice if queasiness starts before eating a single spoon.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel on learning the story about the cook was wrong?
qa.a: Darshan might feel embarrassed for spreading it, and perhaps sorry for the new cook, whose upma was blamed for something it didn't cause.

grounding: A teenager feels sick before eating after hearing the mess food causes illness, and the feeling disappears once the rumour is corrected.

passage: On Rekha's first day at the new school in Almora, a senior in the corridor leaned over. 'Don't eat the canteen chole. Half of Class 8 got sick from it last month.' By the lunch bell, Rekha's stomach was already heavy. In the queue, the smell of chole made her throat tighten, and her mouth filled with water. She hadn't taken a single bite. She sat with a plain paratha and pushed the bowl far away. Then Charu, from her bench, dropped down beside her with a sports-day form. 'Help me fill this? I can't spell "javelin".' They laughed over the spelling. Without thinking, Rekha dipped her paratha in Charu's chole and ate half of it. Only when she saw the empty bowl did she remember. Her stomach gave a small lurch, then settled. She felt completely fine.

qa.q: What did the senior tell Rekha about the canteen chole?
qa.a: The senior said, 'Don't eat the canteen chole. Half of Class 8 got sick from it last month.'

qa.q: Why did Rekha's stomach feel heavy before she had eaten anything?
qa.a: She was anxious after the senior's warning, and expecting to feel ill was enough to make her stomach and throat react.

qa.q: What could Rekha do the next time she hears a warning like that?
qa.a: She could check whether it's true, for example by asking someone who eats there, before her worry turns into feeling sick.

qa.q: How might Charu see Rekha pushing the bowl away and then eating from hers?
qa.a: Charu might find it funny, since Rekha was fine eating chole once she was busy laughing and not thinking about the warning.

grounding: On her first day a teenage girl feels sick at the smell of canteen food she was warned about before eating any, and is fine once distracted.

passage: In the school cafeteria in Uppsala, Oskar stood in line with his tray while Sofia whispered, 'Don't take the fish soup. The whole of 9B was sick after it on Monday.' He looked at the big steel pot. The steam suddenly seemed thick and oily. By the time he reached the counter his stomach was churning, and he felt a sour taste at the back of his mouth. He took bread and a plain boiled potato instead. But even with the potato, the churning stayed. That was odd. The potato was just a potato. He looked across and saw Sofia's friend Emil eating a full bowl of the soup and laughing. Oskar put his fork down. His stomach still felt tight all through maths, and he kept thinking about the soup, not the numbers on the board.

qa.q: What did Sofia say about the fish soup?
qa.a: Sofia whispered that the whole of 9B was sick after it on Monday.

qa.q: Why did Oskar's stomach keep churning even while eating the plain potato?
qa.a: The worry from Sofia's warning was causing the churning, not the food, so it stayed even with something he knew was safe.

qa.q: What could Oskar do next time a food rumour makes him feel sick?
qa.a: He could notice that the feeling started before eating anything and ask a teacher or the cafeteria staff whether anyone really got sick.

qa.q: How might Emil's easy meal look to Oskar?
qa.a: Seeing Emil eat a full bowl and laugh might make Oskar wonder whether the rumour was true, and feel a bit silly about his fear.

grounding: A teenage boy starts feeling nauseous after hearing a cafeteria rumour, before eating, and the feeling stays even with safe food.

passage:
In the residential school outside the town, lunch was always dal, rice and one sabzi. On Monday, Kamal leaned across the bench and whispered, "Don't eat the dal. Three boys from Class 9 got sick from it yesterday."
Manoj looked at his plate. Suddenly the smell seemed wrong. His stomach turned. He felt a wave of sickness rise before he had even lifted the spoon.
"I'm not hungry," he said, pushing the plate away. He sat through the period with a cold sweat on his neck.
At evening study, the warden announced that the Class 9 boys had eaten street pakoras on their outing; nothing to do with the mess. Manoj felt his stomach unknot almost at once. At dinner he ate two helpings of the same dal.

qa.q: What had the Class 9 boys actually eaten, according to the warden?
qa.a: They had eaten street pakoras on their outing.

qa.q: Why did Manoj feel sick before even eating?
qa.a: He felt anxious after Kamal's warning, and that fear made the smell seem wrong and created real sickness.

qa.q: What could Manoj do next time he hears a rumour like this?
qa.a: He could check with the warden or mess staff before believing it, and notice whether the feeling started with the rumour rather than the food.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel after the warden's announcement?
qa.a: Kamal might feel sheepish, realising the whispered rumour made Manoj miss lunch for nothing.

grounding: A teenager told that the mess food made people sick feels nauseous before eating, showing anxious expectation creating real sensations.

passage:
Friday was fish-pie day in the school canteen in Galway. As Liam queued, his friend Rafael turned round. "Heard someone threw up after the fish pie last week. Just saying."
Liam took the plate anyway. At the table, he stared at it. The steam smelled heavy. His throat tightened, and a queasy feeling spread under his ribs. He ate one forkful and put the fork down.
"You alright?" Rafael asked. "You've gone pale."
"I feel sick. Must be the fish."
But Rafael was already halfway through his own plate, totally fine. So were the twenty other people at the long table.
Liam looked around, confused. In biology they'd talked about the nocebo effect once. He hadn't thought it could happen to him over a fish pie.

qa.q: What day was fish-pie day in the canteen?
qa.a: Friday was fish-pie day.

qa.q: What made Liam's throat tighten as he stared at the plate?
qa.a: He felt anxious because of Rafael's rumour, and that fear turned into a real queasy feeling before the food could have done anything.

qa.q: What could Liam try to separate the rumour from his body's reaction?
qa.a: He could notice that everyone else was fine, take a few calm breaths and, if he still felt unwell, tell a teacher rather than blaming the food.

qa.q: How might Rafael see his own comment after watching Liam go pale?
qa.a: Rafael might feel a little guilty, realising that a passing remark made his friend feel sick while he himself was fine.

grounding: A teenager warned about canteen food feels sick before eating much, while others are fine, showing the nocebo effect.

passage:
On the second day of the summer football camp at the sports complex, Maria sat down beside Ujjwal in the dining hall. "The paneer here gave my cousin food poisoning last year," she said.
Ujjwal looked at the paneer curry on his tray. It looked fine. But his stomach gave a slow roll. He felt hot. By the time he picked up a roti, he was sure he was going to be sick.
He went outside and sat on the steps, breathing hard. The coach found him there. "What's wrong?"
"The paneer. Maria said it's bad."
The coach sat beside him. "Forty kids ate it yesterday. All fine. Sit a bit, and if you still feel unwell we'll call the camp doctor."
Ten minutes later, the rolling had faded. He went back in, a little embarrassed, and ate the roti.

qa.q: How many kids had eaten the paneer yesterday, according to the coach?
qa.a: Forty kids ate it yesterday.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as he sat on the steps?
qa.a: He felt anxious and sick, sure the paneer would make him ill because of what Maria said.

qa.q: Which part of the coach's response helped?
qa.a: The coach stayed calm, gave facts about the forty kids, and offered to call the camp doctor if Ujjwal still felt unwell.

qa.q: How might Maria feel if she found out what happened?
qa.a: Maria might feel sorry, seeing that her story about her cousin made Ujjwal feel ill before he ate anything.

grounding: A teenager told the camp food caused sickness feels ill before eating, and the feeling fades once he is calmly reassured.

passage:
Dear Jasleen,
You'll laugh at this. On Monday a senior told us the canteen chole had "made half of Class 12 sick" last week. On Tuesday I stood in the queue and my stomach started to turn before I even reached the counter. By the time I sat down I felt properly queasy, sweaty palms and all. I pushed the plate away.
Then Rukhsar, who'd been absent on Monday and hadn't heard anything, finished her whole plate happily. And the canteen uncle said there had been no complaints at all.
Our biology teacher calls it the nocebo effect: expecting to feel ill can make you feel ill. It felt SO real, though. I still haven't had the chole.
Write back soon!
Kavitha

qa.q: What did the senior say about the canteen chole?
qa.a: That it had "made half of Class 12 sick" last week.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling in the canteen queue?
qa.a: Kavitha felt anxious and queasy, the rumour turning the stomach before any food was eaten.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do before trusting the next food rumour?
qa.a: Check the facts first, such as asking the canteen staff or friends who ate it, and notice how worry itself can churn the stomach.

qa.q: How was lunch different for Rukhsar?
qa.a: Rukhsar hadn't heard the rumour, so she enjoyed the same chole without feeling ill.

grounding: A teenager's letter describes feeling nauseous before eating because of a canteen rumour, showing how anxious expectation can create real sensations.

passage:
Chetan, here's the embarrassing part of the school trip. We stopped at this highway dhaba, and before we got down, Arora sir said, "Careful, boys, last year's batch got food poisoning here." Now, I'm Zubin, I eat everything, you know that. But the moment I saw the dal, my throat went tight. I could feel the bus still swaying in my stomach. I was sure it was already happening. I sat outside with a bottle of water while everyone ate.
Then on the bus I found out sir meant a different dhaba, one on the other road. Nobody got sick. Not one person. And the second he said that, the nausea just left. That's the scary bit, right? It was only my head. But it felt like my stomach.

qa.q: What did Arora sir say about the dhaba?
qa.a: That last year's batch got food poisoning here.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when the nausea left?
qa.a: Zubin felt relieved but also unsettled, surprised that a worry alone had felt so physical.

qa.q: What could Zubin do next time a warning makes the stomach tighten?
qa.a: Check which place or food the warning is really about before deciding, and remember that expectation can create real sensations.

qa.q: How might Arora sir feel on learning the effect of his warning?
qa.a: He might feel surprised and a bit sorry that his vague warning made a student feel ill and skip lunch.

grounding: A teenager describes feeling sick at a dhaba purely because of a warning, and the nausea vanishing once the warning turned out to be about somewhere else.

passage:
Dolma, you're scared of the canteen food because of what your friends say? Let your Pala, your father, tell you something. I'm Jagdish. When I was sixteen, in the Dehradun hostel, a rumour went round that the Thursday rajma made people sick.
Every Thursday, I'd sit in front of my plate and my stomach would start turning. Before the first bite! Once I felt so sick I went back to my room without eating.
Then one Thursday, the cook changed the day. Rajma came on Tuesday instead, and nobody knew. I ate two plates and felt fine.
When I found out, I laughed. The rumour had made me sick, not the rajma.

qa.q: Which day was the rajma said to make people sick?
qa.a: The Thursday rajma.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish's stomach start turning before the first bite?
qa.a: Jagdish felt anxious about the rumour, and expecting to feel sick brought on real nausea.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jagdish's story?
qa.a: Eating rajma on Tuesday without knowing and feeling fine, which showed the rumour, not the food, was making him sick.

qa.q: How might the cook have felt about the rumour?
qa.a: The cook may have felt hurt or frustrated that people blamed the rajma without cause.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a teenager feeling nauseous before eating because of a rumour about the food, an example of the nocebo effect.

passage:
It was the day of the maths board exam, and Francis had twenty minutes to eat before the bus. His friend Anjali whispered, leaning over her tray, "Don't eat the canteen poha. Someone in 10B threw up yesterday."
Francis looked at his plate. Suddenly his stomach felt tight and queasy. He pushed the plate away. By the time he reached the exam hall, he felt sick and weak.
At lunch break, the canteen aunty said the boy in 10B had a fever from home, not the poha. Nobody else was ill.
Francis felt foolish. His stomach settled almost at once. He ate a banana and went back in feeling fine.

qa.q: How long did Francis have to eat before the bus?
qa.a: He had twenty minutes to eat.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel sick before even eating?
qa.a: He felt anxious after Anjali's warning, and expecting to feel ill created real nausea.

qa.q: What could Francis do the next time he hears such a rumour?
qa.a: He could check the facts first, like asking the canteen staff, before letting worry make him feel sick.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when she learns the truth?
qa.a: Anjali may feel a bit guilty for spreading the rumour on exam day.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling nauseous before eating because of a rumour about canteen food, as anxious expectation creates real sensations.

passage:
Ojas's school in Indore had a new canteen. On the first day, Ayesha said at the gate, "My cousin says the samosas there make everyone sick."
At lunch, Ojas stared at his samosa. He hadn't bitten it, but his stomach already felt heavy and strange. He took one small bite and felt worse. He ate nothing else.
All afternoon he felt queasy. At home he told his mother, "The canteen food made me sick."
"You ate one bite?"
"Yes."
The next day, the class teacher said the canteen had passed its inspection and nobody had fallen ill. Ojas remembered how sick he'd felt before even biting.

qa.q: What did Ayesha's cousin say about the samosas?
qa.a: The cousin said the samosas make everyone sick.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling as he stared at his samosa?
qa.a: He felt anxious and queasy, with his stomach heavy before he even bit it.

qa.q: What could Ojas learn from this?
qa.a: That worry can create real sensations, so checking facts before believing a rumour can save him a bad afternoon.

qa.q: How might Ojas's mother see his story?
qa.a: She is probably puzzled and a bit amused that one bite made him feel so sick, suspecting the worry was the cause.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling sick before eating because of a rumour about canteen food, showing the nocebo effect.

passage: The monsoon had made the canteen floor muddy. "Don't eat the rajma," Sangeeta whispered as they queued. "Why?" asked Nandini. "A girl in 10B said it made half her class sick last week." "Seriously?" Nandini looked at her plate. Suddenly the smell seemed off. "I feel a bit sick already." "You haven't even eaten it!" "I know, but my stomach's turning." She pushed the plate away. "Did anyone actually get sick?" Sangeeta shrugged. "That's what she said." The canteen uncle overheard. "Beta, the health inspector came yesterday. All fine." Nandini took a small bite, cautiously. The queasy feeling slowly faded. "Weird," she said. "I really felt it."

qa.q: What dish did Sangeeta warn Nandini about?
qa.a: The rajma.

qa.q: Why did Nandini feel sick before eating?
qa.a: She felt anxious after hearing the rumour, and that worry made her stomach turn as if the food were already making her ill.

qa.q: What could Nandini do next time she hears a rumour like this?
qa.a: Check the facts first, as the canteen uncle's news helped, before letting worry decide how she feels.

qa.q: How might the canteen uncle feel overhearing the girls?

grounding: Illustrates a teenager feeling nauseous from an anxious expectation before eating, the nocebo effect.
